shell:
Full-stack practice

Learning Path

The order to follow, one step at a time. Each step names one action and opens the place where it is done on the Stack Map and Labs page.

Units 0 to 2 are built and can be done now. Units 3 to 13 and the electives are planned, and each one lists what exists for it today.

Open Stack Map and Labs

Next step

The steps are listed below, in order.

The ticks could not be saved. They last until this page is closed.

  1. 0Unit 0: Workbench, built
  2. 1Unit 1: Running stack, built
  3. 2Unit 2: Background jobs, built
  4. 3Unit 3: Outside APIs, planned
  5. 4Unit 4: Data, planned

  • 0built, can be done now

How the steps work
Read
Read a section of a lab or a document.
See
Look at a figure, or use an interactive view.
Do
Run the steps or exercises of a lab on your own machine.
Check
Answer in your own words without the page, then compare with the answers.

Tick a step when it is done. The page then shows the next one at the top. A step marked Optional is not counted.

The practice project

From unit 3 on, one small project grows with each unit: a sync service. It pulls records from an outside API into PostgreSQL, keeps them current and shows their status. An example of the records is the issues of a public repository.

The practice API is the GitHub REST API. It is free and it returns results in pages. Its limit without a token is 60 requests an hour, which is low enough to reach on purpose.

Units 0 to 2 use the notes application of Lab 1.

If you use an AI assistant
  1. Lab steps: Make the first attempt without the assistant. Predict, run, read the error. Then ask the assistant to explain, not to fix.
  2. Build tasks: The assistant writes. You write the specification and the checks first, ask for one change at a time, and read every changed file before you run it.
  3. By hand: All SQL in unit 4, and one small edit in every lab.
  4. Debugging: State your own guess at the cause before you ask.
  5. Setup: Use a mode that asks before it runs commands, lab-only credentials, and a rule that blocks reading .env.

Every Do step in units 0 to 2 can be done without an assistant.

How the labs were checked

Lab 1 and Lab 2 were run in containers on Linux on October 11, 2026, with substitute images. The image build, the official images and Windows with WSL have not been run. If a step behaves differently on your machine, note the step and the exact output.

Version 1, October 11, 2026. Ticks are saved to your account on the server. They follow you to any browser or device you open this with.

units.name: Background jobs: queues and workers
units.html:
2Unit 2: Background jobs: queues and workersBuilt
Where
Lab 2 on the Stack Map and Labs page
Time
About an hour for Part A and about an hour for Part B. Both are estimates.
Done when
Parts A and B are done, and you have answered the eight questions under Check yourself.

You will be able to

  • Name the producer, the broker, the task library and the worker in a stack, and say which part tracks unfinished jobs.
  • Say what happens to a running job when its worker is stopped, when it is killed, and when Redis restarts.
  • Say what a time limit and a retry do, and what ends a job that never succeeds.
  • Make a job safe to run twice.

Steps

  1. Read
    Overview tab: what the lab covers, what it needs from Lab 1, and the order of its parts.Open Lab 2, Overview tab
  2. Read
    Concepts tab: the summary, then section 1, the parts and how they stack.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  3. See
    Concepts tab, section 1: the figure of the three stacks. In each column, find the part that tracks unfinished jobs.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  4. Do
    Part A, exercises A1 to A4: follow one job through Redis, let jobs wait, stop the worker during a job, kill the worker during a job. A4 includes a wait of more than three minutes.Open Lab 2, Part A tab
  5. Read
    Concepts tab, section 6, when a worker dies during a job, with the figure that compares stop and kill.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  6. Do
    Part A, exercises A6 and A7: restart and kill Redis while jobs wait, and run two workers on one queue. A5 is optional.Open Lab 2, Part A tab
  7. Do
    Add-on tab, steps 1 to 3: write the add-on's files, go to the project folder, then add the table, set the 30-second time limit, rebuild and check.Open Lab 2, Add-on tab
  8. Read
    Concepts tab, section 7, making a job safe to repeat.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  9. Do
    Part B, exercises B1 to B3: a job that runs past its time limit, one job with two effects, and the same job made safe to repeat.Open Lab 2, Part B tab
  10. Do
    Part B, exercises B4 and B5: retries with a growing delay, and a second queue for light jobs.Open Lab 2, Part B tab
  11. Read
    Concepts tab, sections 8 and 9: writing to two systems and the outbox, with its figure, and what is not covered yet.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  12. Check
    Build and check tab, Check yourself: answer the eight questions in your own words, then open each answer.Open Lab 2, Build and check tab
  13. DoOptional
    Build and check tab: rebuild Part B with an AI coding tool. Parts A and B do not depend on it.Open Lab 2, Build and check tab

units.name: Reliability between systems: the outbox, a status the application owns, a payment with an outside processor
units.html:
6Unit 6: Reliability between systems: the outbox, a status the application owns, a payment with an outside processorPlanned
Status
Planned. The lab is not built.
Adds to the project
The pull job is queued through an outbox, and each run has a status row that the application owns.

You will be able to

  • Save a row and queue its job so that the two cannot disagree.
  • Keep a job status that the application owns, and mark a job as lost when its worker was killed.
  • Recover a payment after a stop at any step, with one charge.

Planned labs

  • Queues: the outbox. Save a row and queue its job so that the two cannot disagree: write an outbox row in the same transaction, and let a relay send it to the queue.
  • Queues: a job status the application owns, and a sweeper. Keep a status row with a heartbeat for each job, and add a scheduled sweeper that marks a job as lost when its worker was killed.
  • Queues: a payment with an outside processor. Record each step of a payment, stop the worker after each one, and use an idempotency key so that recovery leaves one charge.

Available now

    Lab 2, Concepts tab, section 8: the figure Where the outbox fits.Open Lab 2, Concepts tab
  2. ReadOptional

units.name: Electives
units.html:
EElectivesPlanned

Topics for a larger system. They are added when the project needs them and are not part of the first pass.

Planned labs

  • Queues: RabbitMQ beside arq. Run RabbitMQ's work queue tutorials, stop a worker during a task, and watch the broker hand the message to another worker.
  • Queues: SQS behavior with ElasticMQ. See a visibility timeout and a dead-letter queue on an SQS-compatible server in a container, with no AWS account.
  • Queues: queue depth as a scaling signal. Print the queue length while jobs arrive faster than one worker finishes them, and decide from the numbers when to add a worker.
  • Connection pooling with PgBouncer. Run PostgreSQL out of connections under load, then put a pooler in front of it.
  • Read replicas and replication lag. Add a streaming replica, send reads to it, and measure how often a read misses a recent write.
  • Partitioning and sharding. Partition a table inside PostgreSQL, then distribute it across nodes and choose the key.
  • Schema changes without downtime. Check a migration for locking problems, apply an expand-and-contract change, and rehearse a cutover between two databases.
  • WebSockets and server-sent events behind a proxy. Put nginx in front of the API and see the idle timeout and buffering that do not show up on localhost.
  • Load and fault injection. Generate load, add latency and dropped connections between services, and record what fails first.
  • CDN and HTTP caching. Put a CDN in front of the API and read its cache status header. Needs a domain name.

Available now

  1. SeeOptional
    Sharding view, Consistent hashing ring tab.Open Sharding view, Consistent hashing ring tab
  2. SeeOptional
    Real-time and WebSockets view, Connection lifecycle tab.Open Real-time and WebSockets view, Connection lifecycle tab
  3. SeeOptional
    Capacity math view, Reference numbers tab.Open Capacity math view, Reference numbers tab
